Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Multiple Linear Regression SA: W 08 2 / 72Introduction, Example
Job for statistician of a company: Analysis, to work out stra tegy how
to increase sales of a certain product
Company provides data on advertising budget and sales
Data set Advertising consists of:
◮sales of this product in 200 diﬀerent markets
◮Advertising budget of this product in these markets for thre e diﬀerent
media: TV,radio andnewspaper
Code:

head(adv, 3)

Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Multiple Linear Regression SA: W 08 4 / 72For company not possible to directly increase sales of the pr oduct
But it can control advertising spending in the three media
Aim: Establish a link between advertising and sales so that c ompanies
can adjust their advertising budgets to indirectly increas e sales
Aim: Develop a model as accurately as possible, so that on the basis
of the three media budgets the sale of the product can be predicted
TV: Clear relationship between advertising and sales of produ ct
The more money invested in advertising, the greater the sale s ﬁgures
Question: What form does this relationship take?
newspaper : No relationship at all: No need for newspaper advertising
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Multiple Linear Regression SA: W 08 5 / 72Mathematical view: Look for function fwhich determines the sale Y
depending on the advertising budgets X1(TV),X2(radio ) and X3
(newspaper ):
Y≈f(X1,X2,X3)
Relationship above: No equal sign, since scatter plots do not
represent graphs of a function
Function fcan only display the relationship between X1,X2,X3and
Y approximately
Notation:
◮Variable Y:Response variable
◮X1,X2andX3:Predictors ,explanatory variable
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Multiple Linear Regression SA: W 08 6 / 72Generally: Quantitative response variable Yandpdiﬀerent predictors
X1,X2, . . . , Xp
Assume: There is somehow a relationship between Yand
X1,X2, . . . , Xp
General form:
Y=f(X1,X2, . . . , Xp) +ε
fﬁxed but unknown function of X1,X2, . . . , Xp
Quantity ε:Random error term independent of X1,X2, . . . , Xpwith
mean
Meaning of error term ε: Following example

Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Multiple Linear Regression SA: W 08 8 / 72But: Function fwhich links predictors and response variables, usually
unknown
In this situation: Estimate f from the data
Data set simulated: Function fknown (blue curve) in right ﬁgure
Some observations are above, others below the blue curve
Red vertical lines: Represent the error term ε
Overall, errors have an empirical mean close to 0
Aim of the regression: Estimate function f
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Multiple Linear Regression SA: W 08 9 / 72Estimation in stochastics: Calculation of values
Estimation is an approximation of true quantity
Estimated quantity is marked with hat /hatwide
/hatwideY: Estimate of unknown quantity Y
/hatwidef: Estimate of unknown function f
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Multiple Linear Regression SA: W 08 10 / 72Example
Predictors X1,X2, . . . , Xp: Values of various characteristics of a blood
sample that the patient’s family doctor can determine in his laboratory
Response variable Y: Measure of the risk that the patient will suﬀer
severe side eﬀects when using a particular drug
Physician: Wants to predict Ybased on X1,X2, . . . , Xpwhen
prescribing a drug Yso that he does not prescribe a drug to patients
who are at high risk for side eﬀects of this drug - i.e. where Yis large
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Multiple Linear Regression SA: W 08 11 / 72Questions for example of the advertising
Which media contribute to the sale of the product?
Which media have the greatest inﬂuence on sales ?
What increase in sales does a particular increase in TV adver tising
result in?
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Multiple Linear Regression SA: W 08 12 / 72Estimate of f
Several procedures to estimate f
Here only parametric method
Procedure:
◮Assume functional form of f
◮Simplest assumption: flinear in X1,X2, . . . , Xp:
f(X1,X2, . . . , Xp) =β0+β1X1+β2X2+. . .+βpXp
◮Choice of model: Procedure that ﬁts the data into the model best
◮Linear Model: Estimate parameter β0, β1, . . . β p
◮Parameter so that
Y≈β0+β1X1+β2X2+. . .+βpXp
◮Most common method for determining β0, β1, . . . β p:Least squares
method
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Multiple Linear Regression SA: W 08 13 / 72Examples
Example advertising : Linear model:
Sales ≈β0+β1·TV+β2·radio +β3·newspaper
Example Income : Linear model:
Income ≈β0+β1·Education

Data set income :

10 12 14 16 18 20 2220 40 60 80

From data: Linear model (top left):
f(X) =β0+β1X
Also cubic model (polynomial 3rd degree) possible (top righ t):
f(X) =β0+β1X+β2X2+β3X3
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Multiple Linear Regression SA: W 08 16 / 72Many other models conceivable
But which is the “correct” one?
Wrong question
Function funknown: It is up to us to choose the “best” model
Statistics: Assisting in decision-making
Which model is the “better” one in our example?
Cubic model seems to ﬁt better, but is more complicated
Simpler linear model (slightly less accurate) has an advant age: The
parameters β0andβ1can be interpreted geometrically:
◮β0is the yintercept
◮β1the slope of line
Parameters in cubic model are notinterpretable (except β0)
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Multiple Linear Regression SA: W 08 17 / 72Remarks
More complicated models do nothave to be the better models
Phenomenon: Overﬁtting

Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Multiple Linear Regression SA: W 08 21 / 72Simple regression model
Simple linear regression : Very simple procedure to obtain a
quantitative output Yon the basis of a single predictors X
Assumption: Approximately linear relationship between XandY
Mathematically: Linear relationship:
Y≈β0+β1X
„≈” stands for „is approximately modelled by”
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Multiple Linear Regression SA: W 08 22 / 72Example
Example Advertising : Quantity XTVand quantity Ysales
According to the linear regression model, it follows
sales ≈β0+β1·TV
Variables β0andβ1are unknown constants representing the intercept
and slope of the linear model
β0andβ1:Coeﬃcients orparameters of model
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Multiple Linear Regression SA: W 08 23 / 72Coeﬃcients are estimated from the given data
Estimates/hatwideβ0and/hatwideβ1for the model coeﬃcients
If these coeﬃcients are known, future sales can be predicted on the
basis of a speciﬁc advertising budget for TV
Calculation by means of:
/hatwidey=/hatwideβ0+/hatwideβ1x
where /hatwideydenotes the prediction of Ybased on the input X=x

Most common hypothesis test: Testing the null hypothesis
H0: There is norelationship between XandY
Alternative hypothesis
HA: There is arelationship between XandY
Mathematically:
H0:β1= 0
Alternative:
HA:β1/negationslash= 0

Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Multiple Linear Regression SA: W 08 30 / 72Evaluation of the accuracy of the model: R2
Null hypothesis rejected: To what extent does the model ﬁt the data?

Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Multiple Linear Regression SA: W 08 31 / 72Accuracy of linear regression estimated by the residual standard error
(RSE) and the R2statistics
R2more important
R2-statistics: Value between 0 and 1
It indicates to what proportion of the variability in Yis explained by
Xusing the model
Value close to 1: A large proportion of the variability is exp lained by
the regression. The model therefore describes the data very well.
Value close to 0: Regression does not explain variability of response
variable
Again: Graphical “derivation” (lecture notes)
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Multiple Linear Regression SA: W 08 32 / 72Remarks:
Empirical correlation only indicates the accuracy of linear regressions
R2can be used for anyregression
Standard interpretation of R2: “Proportion of the variability which is
explained by the model”
However: Pretty useless
See https://data.library.virginia.edu/is-r-squared-usel ess/?s=03
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Multiple Linear Regression SA: W 08 33 / 72Example
In example of TV advertising the R2value is 0 .61
summary (lm(Sales ~TV))$r.squared
## [1] 0.6118751
Thus almost two thirds of the variability in Sales is explained by TV
with linear regression
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Multiple Linear Regression SA: W 08 34 / 72Multiple Linear Regression
Simple linear regression: Useful procedure to predict outp ut based on
onesingle predictor
In practice: Output often depends on more than one predictor
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Multiple Linear Regression SA: W 08 35 / 72Example
Dataset Advertising : Have seen relationship between TVadvertising
andSales
Data on advertising for Radio andNewspaper also available
Question: Do one or both of these advertising expenses aﬀect sales?
Extend analysis of sales ﬁgures: Consider both additional i nputs

Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Multiple Linear Regression SA: W 08 38 / 72Separate simple linear regressions: Not satisfactory
First: Not clear how to make a prediction for sales for given v alues of
three predictors:
◮Each input linked to sales by diﬀerent regression equation
Second: Each of three regression equations ignores other tw o
predictors for determining coeﬃcients
May lead to very misleading estimates of eﬀect on sales of adv ertising
expenses for each medium if three predictors are correlated
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Multiple Linear Regression SA: W 08 39 / 72Better: All predictors directly taken into account
Each predictor is assigned ownslope coeﬃcient in oneequation
General: pdiﬀerent predictors
Multiple linear regression model :
Y=β0+β1X1+β2X2+. . .+βpXp+ε
Xj:j-th predictor
βj: Relationship between thispredictor and response variable Y
βj: Average change of response variable when changing Xjby one
unit, if all other predictors are kept constant
In other words: Slope in direction of Xj
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Multiple Linear Regression SA: W 08 40 / 72Example
Multiple linear regression model for dataset Advertising :
Sales =β0+β1·TV+β2·Radio +β3·Newspaper +ε
So:
Sales ≈β0+β1·TV+β2·Radio +β3·Newspaper
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Multiple Linear Regression SA: W 08 41 / 72Multiple linear model generalises simple linear model
Calculations and interpretations for multiple model simil ar, although
usually more complicated than linear model
Graphical methods: Virtually no use for multiple linear reg ression
Data points for previous example: Not possible, as three axe s are
already needed for predictors

Determine plane such that sum of squares of distances of data points

Lines:

◮Red: Points below plane
Diﬀerences from point to plane: Residuals
Use again: Least squares method

Based on estimates, one can make predictions:

Estimate parameters: Use again least squares method

Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Multiple Linear Regression SA: W 08 53 / 72Coeﬃcient of separate simple linear regressions in slide 38
Slopes of multiple linear regression for TVandRadio very similar:
◮TV: 0.46 (multiple), 0.48 (single)
◮Radio : 0.189 (multiple), 0.203 (single)

◮Simple: 0.055 (not equal to 0)
◮Multiple: −0.001 (almost equal to 0)

◮Simple: <0.0001 (highly signiﬁcant)
◮Multiple: 0 .86 (far from being signiﬁcant)
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Multiple Linear Regression SA: W 08 54 / 72Simple and multiple regression coeﬃcients can be very diﬀer ent
Simple regression: Slope indicates change in response Sales when
spending CHF 1000 more on newspaper advertising, while othe r two
predictors TVandRadio areignored
Multiple linear regression: Slope for Newspaper describes change in
response Sales when spending CHF 1000 more on newspaper
advertising, while other two predictors TVandradio are hold
constant
Does it make sense that multiple regression does not suggest a
relationship between Sales andNewspaper , but simple regression
implies opposite?

Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Multiple Linear Regression SA: W 08 56 / 72Correlation coeﬃcient Radio andNewspaper : 0.35
What does this mean?
Shows a tendency to invest more in advertising for Newspaper when
advertising expenses for Radio is increased
Assume: Multiple regression model correct
Expenses on Newspaper : No direct inﬂuence on Sales
Advertising expenses for Radio : Higher sales
In markets where more is invested in radio advertising, expe nses on
Newspaper is also higher, as correlation coeﬃcients of 0 .35
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Multiple Linear Regression SA: W 08 57 / 72Simple linear regression: Only correlation between Newspaper and
Sales , whereby for higher values of Newspaper also higher values of
Sales are observed
Simple linear regression only “sees” increase in Sales
But: Newspaper advertising does notinﬂuences sales
Higher values for Newspaper due to correlation also result in higher
values for Radio :This quantity inﬂuences Sales
Newspaper “takes credit” for success of Radio onSales
This result conﬂicts with intuition
Occurs frequently in real situations
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Multiple Linear Regression SA: W 08 58 / 72Absurd example
Simple regression: Relationship between shark attacks and ice cream
sales on a given beach
The greater the ice cream sales, the more frequent shark atta cks
Absurd idea: Ban ice cream sales on this beach so that there ar e no
more shark attacks
But where is the connection?
Reality: In hot weather more people come to beach →more ice
cream sales →more shark attacks
Confounder: Temperature
Multiple regression model of shark attacks with ice cream sa lesand
